name: Spinal Dermal Sinus

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Radiological Diagnostic Criteria for Spinal Dermal Sinus

criteria.description: Presence of a midline cutaneous pit or dimple along the spinal axis with an identifiable sinus tract
MRI evidence of a tract extending from skin surface to spinal canal or intradural space
Neurological deficits consistent with spinal cord tethering or infection
Associated cutaneous stigmata such as hypertrichosis, hemangioma, or subcutaneous lipoma near the sinus

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of a visible sinus tract with MRI confirmation of the tract extending to the spinal canal
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Early diagnosis is critical to prevent neurological deterioration and infection.

pathognomonic.notes: Typically located in the lumbosacral region
searchTerms: skin sinus tract along midline back
skin tract in midline spine area

pathognomonic.symptomName: Recurrent meningitis due to tract infection
pathognomonic.notes: Often caused by bacterial contamination through the sinus

common.notes: Includes lower limb weakness, sensory deficits, and bladder dysfunction

common.symptomName: Cutaneous stigmata adjacent to sinus tract
searchTerms: cutaneous signs adjacent to skin tract

common.notes: May be related to inflammation or tethering

searchTerms: increased muscle tone in lower limbs

occasional.symptomName: Cutaneous infection or abscess formation at sinus site
Scoliosis secondary to spinal cord tethering
searchTerms: curved spine from spinal cord tethering
spinal curvature due to cord pulling
scoliosis caused by spinal cord tension

occasional.notes: Fluid-filled cavities within the spinal cord

rare.symptomName: Sepsis secondary to infected sinus tract
searchTerms: sepsis due to infected skin tract
fluid buildup in brain after meningitis

laboratory: CSF analysis showing pleocytosis and elevated protein in cases of meningitis
Positive bacterial cultures from CSF or sinus tract discharge during infection
imaging: MRI demonstrating sinus tract extending from skin surface to spinal canal
Evidence of tethered cord, syringomyelia, or intradural cysts
genetic: No specific genetic mutations identified; congenital malformation likely multifactorial
other: Physical examination revealing midline cutaneous pit or dimple with possible hair tuft

distinguishingFeatures: Absence of an open sinus tract
Imaging shows bony defect without dermal sinus
Simple sacral dimple without tract extending to spinal canal
Open neural tube defect with exposed spinal cord

redFlags: Progressive neurological deficits including lower limb weakness
Visible midline sinus tract with discharge or signs of infection
references: Barkovich AJ, et al. Pediatric Neuroimaging. 5th ed. 2012.
Talamonti G, et al. Spinal dermal sinus: clinical features and surgical treatment. Neurosurgery. 2007.
